solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Titanic’s crew finally jumping

indicators.note: what comes finally comes at the end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of crew
hopping is jumping about

explanation.surface: The crew of the doomed liner finally leaping overboard as the ship goes down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Titanic' with its capital looks like the ship, but here it is just the adjective meaning enormous; the 's is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal or literary ways of describing something of colossal, huge size.

clue.text: Attempt to keep French down with heroin

blocks.note: to keep something is to have it
'à bas' is the French cry meaning 'down with'
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: Someone trying to hold back a French person who is going under with a heroin habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down with' reads as 'together with', but it belongs to 'French': à bas is the French slogan 'down with'.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a bash is an informal British idiom for making a try or giving something a go.

clue.text: Grill family’s fruit

blocks.note: to grill or pump someone is to question them hard for information
kin are one's family

explanation.surface: A family barbecuing the fruit from their garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grill' suggests cooking, but it is the interrogation sense, as a detective grills a suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically a pumpkin is a fruit, the large seed-bearing gourd of a squash plant.

clue.text: Writer is disturbed by book being oddly ignored

indicators.note: something disturbed by an intruder has that intruder thrust into its middle
ignoring the odd-numbered letters leaves only the even ones in place

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for book
the second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: An author unsettled because a book of theirs is being overlooked in a strange way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like 'strangely', but it means lose the odd letters, leaving the even ones of 'being'.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian playwright of A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler, so a writer by example.

clue.text: Follow up idol

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely

explanation.surface: An instruction to pursue your hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follow up' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'up' is separate and turns the word over in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is an object or figure worshipped as a deity, and the word is used loosely for any worshipped being.

clue.text: Self-confident lad scoffs endless meal

indicators.note: whoever scoffs food takes it inside, so one piece goes into another
having no end at either side means both outer letters are removed

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
lunch is a meal

explanation.surface: A cocky young man wolfing down a meal that never seems to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' strips both ends of the meal, not just the last letter; 'scoffs' means eats greedily, and what is eaten goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A bouncy person is lively and buoyantly assured, full of cheerful self-assurance.

clue.text: Tractor shifted boulder containing separate traces of lead and zinc

indicators.note: things that are shifted are moved about, so the letters are rearranged
to contain is to hold inside, so other letters are set within
a trace is the barest hint, so one opening letter is kept from each word, and the two go in apart

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of lead
the opening letter of zinc

explanation.surface: A tractor moving a big rock that shows faint signs of lead and zinc ore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Separate' tells you the two single letters go in at different places in the rearranged BOULDER rather than side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulldozer is a heavy tracked tractor fitted with a broad blade for pushing earth and rubble.

clue.text: Dodgy report, arguably lacking introduction

indicators.note: lacking an introduction means the opening letter has gone

blocks.note: a report is the bang of a gun, so arguably a gun sound

explanation.surface: A shaky report whose argument does not stand up, perhaps lacking a proper opening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' is the noise of a gunshot, not a document; 'arguably' admits that GUNSOUND is a made-up compound before its G goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unsound is unreliable or not to be trusted, which is what dodgy means informally.

clue.text: Covering head of injured animal

indicators.note: the head of a word is its top, so only its first letter is kept

blocks.note: a layer laid over something, as of paint or an animal's fur
the first letter of injured

explanation.surface: A vet bandaging the head of a hurt animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covering head' looks like a bandage, but 'Covering' stands alone as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The coati is a raccoon-like mammal of the Americas with a long snout and ringed tail.

clue.text: Cell phone drivers corrupted games, essentially

indicators.note: the essence of something is its heart, so the central letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the central letter of a five-letter word
the fourth of seven letters
the fifth of nine letters
the central letter of a five-letter word

explanation.surface: Mobile phone software that has been hacked to ruin the games on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cell phone' looks like one American phrase, but 'Cell' is the definition, and 'essentially' applies to all four following words, not just the last.
explanation.definitionFit: An ovum is the female reproductive cell, the egg that is fertilised in conception.

clue.text: Cleaner burdens grandpa, for one?

blocks.note: to saddle someone is to burden them with something
an OAP is an old-age pensioner, of whom a grandpa is a typical example

explanation.surface: A cleaner who loads her elderly grandfather with chores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleaner' looks like a person; it is a product. OAP, old-age pensioner, is the British term for a retired person.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddle soap is a mild soap used for cleaning and conditioning leather goods like saddles and boots.

clue.text: American dove, JFK, nicked with a shot

blocks.note: President John F. Kennedy was known as Jack
a shot is a stab, and to be nicked with a stab is to be cut with a blade

explanation.surface: A grim note on the American president, wounded by a shot, cast as a peace-loving dove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dove' looks like the bird or a peacemaker, but it is the American past tense of dive; 'shot' means an attempt or stab, not gunfire.
explanation.definitionFit: To jackknife is to make a dive bending at the waist before straightening, and Americans say dove for dived.

clue.text: Anxious about anger if excited

indicators.note: excited particles move about wildly, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone worried about losing their temper when worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about temper; 'about' belongs with 'Anxious' in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearing something and being worried over it both describe dread of something that might happen.

clue.text: Detach coreless operating system

indicators.note: without a core means the central letter has been cut out

blocks.note: to unfix something is to detach it

explanation.surface: An instruction to remove a hollowed-out piece of computer software.
explanation.walkthrough: The central letter of the five removed is the F.
explanation.definitionFit: Unix is the computer operating system developed at Bell Labs, ancestor of Linux and macOS.

clue.text: Trouble concerning leg when going over tree

indicators.note: going over is turning head over heels, so the string is read backwards

blocks.note: to ail is to trouble
on means concerning, as in a book on birds
gam is slang for a leg

explanation.surface: An injured leg playing up while climbing over a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going over' suggests climbing, but it reverses the whole string. Gam is old American slang for a leg.
explanation.definitionFit: The magnolia is a flowering tree or shrub with large showy white or pink blossoms.

clue.text: Defamatory Aussie demand for classification possibly picked up

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to catch it by ear, and 'possibly' admits the match is approximate

blocks.note: an Australian asking to be classified would say 'label us', with the Aussie vowel making it 'libel us'

explanation.surface: An Australian's insulting call to be pigeonholed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' admits the accent joke: in a broad Australian accent the long A of label slides towards an I sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Libel is written defamation, so a statement that is libellous damages someone's reputation falsely.

clue.text: Unknown helper wearing firm round belt

indicators.note: whoever wears clothing is inside it, so one piece is enclosed by the other
to turn round is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: in algebra unknowns are x, y and z
an aid is a helper, as in a teaching aid
CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A mystery assistant at a company putting on a round belt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round belt' looks like a description, but 'round' reverses the container and 'belt' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The zodiac is the imaginary band of sky through which sun, moon and planets appear to move.

clue.text: Teases topless partner, an easy target

indicators.note: without a top means the first letter, at the head of this down entry, is removed

blocks.note: to taunt is to tease
an ally is a partner

explanation.surface: Mocking a bare-chested companion who is easy to pick on.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aunt Sally is a British pub and fairground game in which sticks are thrown at a dummy's head.
explanation.definitionFit: From that game, an Aunt Sally became an idiom for a person or idea set up to be criticised or attacked.

clue.text: Little boy cuddles that woman’s sweet child

indicators.note: to cuddle is to hold in your arms, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a cub is a young animal, or a boy scout
her is the possessive for that woman

explanation.surface: A small boy hugging a woman's lovable child.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's is part of the pronoun piece, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherub is an angel pictured as a chubby winged infant, so the word is used for any adorable little one.

clue.text: Relative indeed died, or passed on

blocks.note: REL is an abbreviation for relative
aye means yes, indeed
D is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A relative really did die, or as we say, passed on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passed on' looks like a euphemism for 'died'; it is the definition in its other sense of handing a message along.
explanation.definitionFit: To relay a message is to receive it and pass it to the next person in a chain.

clue.text: Annoying girl fills in old Tax Office books

indicators.note: whatever fills in a gap goes inside it, so one piece sits within others

blocks.note: the Inland Revenue was Britain's tax authority until 2005
a girl's name
the New Testament is a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A tiresome young woman completing paperwork at a former tax office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Books' is the crossword convention for NT, New Testament, or OT; here the tax office and the books together form the outer shell.
explanation.definitionFit: An irritant is something that annoys, and the word works as an adjective meaning causing annoyance.

clue.text: Twice ordered around vicious canine without using line

indicators.note: to go around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another
doing without something means leaving it out

blocks.note: to be told is to be ordered to do something
a wolf is a fierce wild dog
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A dog twice commanded to circle a dangerous hound without a lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' sounds like a dog's leash, but it is just the letter L, taken out of the canine before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Twofold and twice both mean two times as much, double in number or amount.

clue.text: After losing son, chap’s empty

indicators.note: after something is lost it is no longer there, so it is taken out

blocks.note: a man's name
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A father left hollow after the death of his son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' reads as an adjective for grief, but it is a verb, as in bailing water from a boat; the 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bail a boat is to scoop water out of it, emptying it by hand.

clue.text: City quartermaster and brigadier initially infiltrating battery

indicators.note: what comes initially comes first, so only opening letters are kept
to infiltrate is to get inside, so these letters go within the others

blocks.note: AA is a standard battery size
the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Army officers in a military city sneaking into an artillery battery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battery' looks military to match the officers, but it means an AA cell.
explanation.definitionFit: Aqaba is Jordan's only port city, on the Red Sea, famously taken by Lawrence of Arabia.

clue.text: Two strokes dropped by leader on 8th hole? Employ course guide

indicators.note: taking two of the pen strokes off a capital E leaves a capital L, so the first letter changes

blocks.note: 8th written out in full
O is shaped like a hole
to employ something is to use it

explanation.surface: A golfer gets a two-shot penalty at the eighth hole, and the guide is told how to play the course.
explanation.walkthrough: Golf terms abound but none is golf: E is drawn with four strokes, and removing the top and middle bars leaves L.
explanation.definitionFit: A lighthouse guides ships on their course by warning them of rocks and marking the safe channel.

clue.text: Tory’s opening dispute involves hospital project

indicators.note: an opening is a start, so only the first letter is kept
to involve something is to take it in, so it goes inside

blocks.note: the first letter of Tory
a row is a quarrel
H is the abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician's first quarrel concerns a hospital-building scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Project' reads as a noun for a scheme, but it is the verb, pronounced differently, meaning to hurl.
explanation.definitionFit: To project something is to hurl or cast it forward through the air.

clue.text: Labour’s successful outcome in the 1950s?

blocks.note: surface reading: an election victory for Britain's Labour Party
setter's reading: the result of a mother's labour, a child born in the post-war population surge

explanation.surface: A political commentator recalling a Labour Party triumph in the post-war decade.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour with a capital suggests the British political party; read it as childbirth, and the successful outcome is a newborn of the boom years.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names people born during the post-war surge in births, roughly 1946 to 1964.

clue.text: Individual marks heralding a third in Linguistics

indicators.note: the third of a series is its number three, so the letter in that position is taken

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for marks, the old German currency
taken as written
the third letter of the word

explanation.surface: A student's grades foretelling a third-class degree in Linguistics.
explanation.walkthrough: A third is the lowest class of British honours degree, but here 'a' is a letter of its own and 'third' points at a position.
explanation.definitionFit: Man is used for a single person, as in 'every man for himself', meaning each individual.

clue.text: Just a scrap of lunch — skipping starter, £25 should cover it

indicators.note: a scrap is a tiny piece, so a single first letter is all that is kept
skipping the starter means the first letter is left out
a covering goes round what it covers, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds
the first letter of lunch

explanation.surface: A tiny lunch with no first course, yet costing twenty-five pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skipping starter' looks like it belongs to the lunch, but it applies to the slang word for £25; 'it' is the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Just and only are adverbs meaning merely or no more than, as in 'just a scrap'.

clue.text: Bother about one’s deceptively spacious transport?

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: drat is a mild exclamation of annoyance
one is, I for one plus S

explanation.surface: Fussing over whether your vehicle is really as roomy as the estate agent claims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deceptively spacious' is estate-agent jargon for a small home; the TARDIS is the Doctor Who time machine, bigger inside than out.
explanation.definitionFit: The Doctor's police-box ship carries people through time and space and is famously larger on the inside.

clue.text: Yank’s never accepting notice, presently

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: noways is an American way of saying not at all
an ad is a notice advertising something

explanation.surface: An American who never takes any notice at the present time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank's' flags the American word, a variant of 'no way' meaning never.
explanation.definitionFit: Presently, in its older and American sense, means at the present time, as nowadays does.
